title: Orsen and the Harvest
premise: Jonah Eastwick, a skeptical property surveyor, is hired to appraise her late grandmother's farmhouse and discovers the appraisal is happening in both directions: the house counts its inhabitants, and every old photograph now shows one extra chair at the table. The house's hunger runs through the dry well on the property, which refills only when it has taken enough of the family — and her scattered relatives, each bound by old debts to the land, are next on the count. As harvest season peaks, Jonah must choose between the duty she owes her family's legacy and the love she feels for the one relative who understands what the house truly wants. In the end, Jonah fills the extra chair herself with a bargain that starves the well dry, saving the family but leaving her forever part of the house's memory.
about_author: Yara Eastwick grew up in rural Ohio surrounded by family farms that had been in the same hands for six generations, where every attic held photographs no one liked to explain. She writes horror about inheritance, houses that remember, and the quiet violence of belonging somewhere you can't leave.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. A surveyor who doesn't believe in anything arrives at her dead grandmother's farmhouse to appraise it for sale. The rooms measure wrong — a hallway longer inside than out. Emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack as the house seems to notice her back.

chapters.title: One Chair Too Many
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Sorting grandma's photos for probate, Jonah finds every family picture now includes an empty wooden chair at the table that wasn't there before. Her cousin Dee swears the chair was always there. Emotional beat: first vertigo of doubt — reality quietly rewriting itself.

chapters.title: Family Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Dee reveals the Eastwicks have kept a ledger since 1911: names, dates, and a column labeled simply 'taken.' Every entry matches a death on the property. Emotional beat: dread dressed up as genealogy; the family has always known something.

chapters.title: The Dry Well
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Inspecting the property, Jonah finds the well bone-dry despite weeks of rain, its stones warm like skin. At the bottom, faintly, someone hums a lullaby grandma used to sing. Emotional beat: the house's appetite made physical and intimate.

chapters.title: Uncle Ray Comes Home
chapters.summary: POV Uncle Ray. The eldest Eastwick returns uninvited, claiming he dreamed the house called him. He sleeps in his childhood room and wakes with dirt under his fingernails he can't explain. Emotional beat: homesickness weaponized; the house luring its own.

chapters.title: Counting Heads
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. The photograph changes again — the chair is no longer empty. A blurred figure sits in it wearing grandma's shawl. That night, Ray sleepwalks to the well and has to be dragged back. Emotional beat: the count has begun, and everyone knows their place in line.

chapters.title: What Grandma Left
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. In a locked root cellar, Jonah finds grandma's journals: instructions for 'keeping the count low,' rituals of salt and naming, and a final unfinished entry — 'when the well refills, it will want' — cut off mid-sentence. Emotional beat: grief curdling into purpose.

chapters.title: Dee's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Desperate to protect her kids, Dee secretly offers the house a trade — herself for a delay. The house accepts too eagerly. Her children begin drawing pictures of mommy sitting in a chair. Emotional beat: maternal love twisted into leverage against her.

chapters.title: The Reunion
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah gathers the scattered Eastwicks under one roof, planning to sell and scatter before the harvest moon. But the house rearranges itself overnight — doors opening into older decades, hallways lined with family portraits whose eyes follow. Emotional beat: unity as trap; gathering them fed the house.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: POV Ray. Ray, half-claimed already, hears the well filling — water rising with voices in it, each voice a taken ancestor. He warns the family: when the well brims, the count completes. Emotional beat: the deadline becomes audible, ticking in water.

chapters.title: Doors That Remember
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Trying to evacuate everyone, Jonah finds exits loop back to the kitchen table, where the extra chair waits. Time stutters; breakfast happens three times. Emotional beat: claustrophobic futility — the house won't release what it's counting.

chapters.title: The First Taken
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Ray vanishes at dusk; his chair appears in the newest photograph, occupied. Dee realizes her bargain bought time with someone else's life and breaks down confessing everything. Emotional beat: guilt detonating; love and betrayal indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Salt and Names
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Following grandma's journal, Jonah performs the naming ritual — speaking each ancestor's true name to bind them against the house. It works until she reaches a name smudged beyond reading, an ancestor deliberately erased from the ledger. Emotional beat: hope undercut by a deliberate omission.

chapters.title: The Erased One
chapters.summary: POV Ray (from within). Ray, half-dissolved into the house's memory, meets the erased ancestor — the first Eastwick, cheated of her name and buried without rites, who taught the house to count. She isn't the villain; she's the wound. Emotional beat: sympathy for the monster's origin.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah and Dee, estranged over the confession, reconcile over grandma's letters — discovering grandma once faced the same choice and chose duty, letting the house take Jonah's father. Emotional beat: inherited sacrifice; the cycle named at last.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: POV Dee. On the harvest moon's eve, the well brims. Water climbs the walls of the house itself, and every mirror shows the table set for dinner with two empty chairs now. Emotional beat: terror at full flood; the count wants more than one.

chapters.title: The Last Supper
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. The house forces the family to the table; plates serve themselves with food tasting of earth and iron. The erased one manifests, offering a deal: give the house a willing heir and the rest go free. Emotional beat: the climax's terrible menu laid bare.

chapters.title: Chair for One
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah volunteers — not from duty but because she finally loves this broken family enough to stay. She speaks her own true name into the well and sits in the extra chair. Emotional beat: love choosing the price duty always demanded.

chapters.title: Draining
chapters.summary: POV Dee. The well drains with a sound like a long exhale. Doors unlock, decades peel away, and the photographs shed their extra chairs one by one. Dee leads the family out at dawn. Emotional beat: release and unbearable cost in the same breath.

chapters.title: What the Surveyor Signed
chapters.summary: POV Dee. Finalizing the sale, Dee finds Jonah's appraisal report completed in Jonah's handwriting — dated fifty years in the future, describing the house as 'occupied, well-maintained, single resident.' Emotional beat: hope shadowed by implication.

chapters.title: Occupied
chapters.summary: POV Jonah (within). Inside the house's memory, Jonah walks endless golden-hour rooms with the erased one, learning the house's whole history. She isn't suffering — she's becoming its keeper, softening its hunger from within. Emotional beat: eerie peace, ambiguous salvation.

chapters.title: The Harvest After
chapters.summary: POV Dee, epilogue. A year later, Dee visits the sold house's new owners, who report it's 'the easiest house they've ever lived in.' In a window photo on their mantel, a woman stands smiling beside the table. Emotional beat: belonging achieved at a price that never stops being paid.
